occupation: Construction Project Labor and Payroll Administrator
role: Labor and payroll administrator at a residential construction project office
headline: The labor and payroll administrator in the project office of a thirty-odd-tower housing development on the east side of Zhengzhou, handling real-name registration, attendance and wage payment for more than six hundred workers, and dreading most the week before payday
unit: The project office of a subsidiary of a provincial state-owned construction group, building a housing development in Zhengzhou as general contractor over a dozen labor subcontracting crews: carpenters, rebar, masonry, plumbing and electrical
level: You can handle the real-name registration platform, attendance checks and wage sheet reviews on your own. When workers crowd into the project office demanding their pay, you still have to call the project manager out
intro: You went straight from university to the construction site, starting as a labor clerk taking workers' fingerprints and signing their contracts, and did that for two years. This project has thirty-odd towers and more than six hundred workers, and what time each of them came through the gate each day, and how much each is owed this month, all passes through your hands. As of today, when the workers say 'the one in the project office who handles the money', they mean you.
salary_note: Estimate: a labor and payroll post in a Zhengzhou general contractor's project office, base pay plus project allowance, comes in a little below the national figure. Allowances are higher when the project is out of town or rushing a deadline; between the end of one project and the start of the next, it's base pay only.

facts.label: Construction Project Labor and Payroll Administrator (current level)
facts.value: 1-4 years, ¥6,375–9,375 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Handling workers who come to the project office demanding unpaid wages

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Registering a newly arrived crew under the real-name system

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: A long queue at the face-recognition gates by the site entrance, workers scanning in one by one. You stand to the side watching the head count on the platform climb to 512, twenty-odd fewer than the crew bosses reported.

Morning meeting at the project office. The project manager says the rebar crew is adding people this week to rush the structure, and you need to get real-name registration and safety training records done today for eighteen new arrivals.

In the prefab office, new workers line up to sign labor contracts. You read the terms out clause by clause. A man in his fifties from Zhoukou can't read; when you finish you ask if he understood, he nods, and presses his thumbprint.

The masonry crew boss brings last month's wage sheet. You check it line by line against the gate attendance and find three people who haven't come on site once this month but have wages on the sheet. You circle them and hand it back.

A bowl of braised noodles at the site canteen, twelve yuan. You take it out to look at the workers' rights notice board by the gate; the labor inspection hotline on it is a little blurred by rain. You take a photo; it needs replacing this afternoon.

You go to the bank to reconcile. This month's labor cost transfer into the dedicated migrant worker wage account has reached seventy percent. You check ID numbers and card numbers on the payment list one by one, afraid of getting a single digit wrong.

A carpenter calls to say his wage card was ¥1,200 short last month. You pull up his attendance and the crew's wage sheet and spend half an hour on it: the crew boss deducted an advance. You arrange for the two of them to sort it out face to face tomorrow.

It's dark. You file today's arrival and departure records and scanned contracts into the ledger. The tower crane lights are still on outside the prefab, and riding your e-bike home past a hot pepper soup shop, you remind yourself to come early tomorrow for a bowl.

ladder.title: Project Labor Clerk / Document Controller
ladder.focus: Help sign contracts, do real-name registration and enter attendance.

ladder.title: Construction Project Labor and Payroll Administrator
ladder.focus: Independently run the project's real-name system, attendance, wage sheet review, payment through the dedicated account, ledgers and the notice board.

ladder.title: Project Labor Manager
ladder.focus: Supervise subcontractors' use of labor, handle unpaid-wage disputes, and deal with inspections.

ladder.title: Company Labor / HR Supervisor
ladder.focus: Run the labor and payroll system and compliance across multiple projects.

ladder.title: Head of Labor Management Department
ladder.focus: The company's labor management policies and risk prevention.

ai_tasks.name: Registering a newly arrived crew under the real-name system
ai_tasks.how: AI can read ID cards and contract details, fill in the platform registration automatically and check that training records are complete. A person has to confirm on site that the face matches the ID, watch that contracts are really signed and really handed out, and decide whether to clear them onto the site.

ai_tasks.name: Checking attendance every day and handling anomalies
ai_tasks.how: AI can compare gate data with what the crews report and flag missed clock-ins and suspected buddy punching automatically. A person goes on site to find out why, judges whether it's a real miss or fraud, and talks it through with the crew boss to correct it.

ai_tasks.name: Reviewing a subcontractor's monthly wage sheet and paying through the dedicated account
ai_tasks.how: AI can cross-check wage sheets against attendance and work quantities in bulk, and screen out abnormal amounts and duplicate names. A person verifies that workers' signatures are genuine, confirms each worker receives the money in person, and answers for the payment review.

ai_tasks.name: Handling workers who come to the project office demanding unpaid wages
ai_tasks.how: AI can help organize attendance and wage records, calculate what's owed and draft mediation documents. Calming the workers, negotiating with the subcontractor, deciding whether the general contractor advances the money and recovers it later: all of that has to be handled face to face by a person who answers for it.

ai_tasks.name: Supporting human resources and construction authority inspections of real-name registration and wage payment
ai_tasks.how: AI can self-check in advance against the inspection list whether ledgers, the dedicated account and public notices are complete, and generate summary materials. A person answers questions at the inspection, explains the situation, puts problems right, and is responsible for the ledgers being true.

ai_tasks.name: Setting up a monthly check of subcontractors' labor
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile each subcontractor's labor, attendance and wage data every month and generate check sheets and risk alerts. A person decides what to focus on, spot-checks on site, calls in subcontractors for talks, and signs the records.

events.e_ghost: In one wage sheet you find five names that never once came on site, all relatives from a crew boss's home village. The project manager talks to the crew boss for an hour, and that month you get glared at around the site more than once.
events.e_spring: The month before Spring Festival is the time you dread most all year. The workers are all waiting for their money to go home, the developer's progress payment keeps not arriving, and every day you run between the project office, company finance and the bank, your phone ringing a hundred times a day.
events.e_paid: The twentieth of the last lunar month, and the whole year's wages have gone through the dedicated account onto the workers' cards. At the project office door you watch them shoulder their woven sacks and go for their trains, and a rebar worker shouts to you: I'll come work for you again next year.
events.e_surround: A subcontractor runs off, and twenty-odd workers crowd around the project office door, some of them very worked up. You stand at the front and read out every person's attendance and wages item by item, reading until dark, and slowly the crowd breaks up.
events.e_dust: Zhengzhou's spring sandstorms plus the dust off the site, and your voice is hoarse from March to May. You put an air purifier in the prefab office, and the filter turns black in two weeks.
events.e_check: The city's human resources and housing and construction authorities come for a joint inspection, going through the real-name ledgers, the dedicated account statements and the notice board, and asking twenty workers face to face whether they've been paid. You went through all the materials three days ahead, and as they leave the inspection team says this project could be a model.
events.e_love: The document controller from the project next door often comes to borrow your printer. The two of you eat lamb braised noodles at the site gate many times, and later go together to see the lights by Ruyi Lake.
events.e_old_worker: An old mason in his sixties is over the age limit and by the rules can't come on site anymore. He begs you to make an exception, saying he has a grandson to support. You can't make one, but you find out about a cleaning job at a housing estate's property management for him.
events.e_platform_ai: The real-name platform is upgraded: AI automatically compares gate attendance with wage sheets and flags buddy punching, missed clock-ins and abnormal amounts. You don't have to check line by line anymore, but it flags dozens a day, and you have to go on site to verify each one.
events.e_rain: A July rainstorm stops the site for a week. With no work, the workers play cards in the prefabs, and all day you're asked: do these days off count for pay? You go through the contracts and the policies and explain to each of them.
events.e_wedding: You hold the wedding back home in Xinyang. Several crew bosses from the project send gifts; you note each one down, and back in Zhengzhou you buy cigarettes and return the favor to each of them.
events.e_dispute_win: A worker reports the project to labor inspection, saying it owes him three months' wages. You produce his gate record for every day, the wage sheets he signed himself and the bank receipts, and in the end it turns out to be a loan between him and his crew boss. When he leaves he doesn't look at you.
events.e_house: You buy a secondhand flat at the edge of Zhengdong New District, the down payment pooled from both families. The day you sign, you start working out how many workers' annual wages it would take to buy, and stop halfway.
events.e_baby: The month your child is born coincides with the project's final settlement. By day you reconcile accounts in the project office, by night you're at the hospital, holding the baby and still answering workers' messages on your phone.
events.e_relocate: This project tops out, and the company moves you to a new one in the Airport Economy Zone, setting up the ledgers, opening the dedicated account and putting up the notice board from scratch. Half the workers on the new project are familiar faces.
events.e_ai_contract: The company brings in an AI tool for contracts and registration: photograph an ID card and the contract details and platform information fill themselves in. Your job becomes watching on site: is the person the one on the ID, did they sign the contract themselves.
events.e_mentor: The labor clerk you trained steadies a dozen workers demanding their wages on her own for the first time. She comes back and tells you she showed them the attendance records page by page, just like you did that day.
events.e_stomach: Years of irregular meals and sleepless nights before payday, and your stomach goes first. The endoscopy shows chronic gastritis; the doctor says less drinking and fewer late nights, and you say on a construction site you can't avoid either.
events.e_developer: The developer on one project pays slower and slower, and the general contractor has to advance wages first and chase the money later. The company decides in a meeting: not a single yuan of wages goes unpaid. The advance request you signed takes two years to recover.
events.e_parent: Your father has a heart attack back home and goes into hospital. You take three days off to go back, and in the ward corridor you phone the project office with instructions about the dedicated account.
events.e_system: The monthly check of subcontractors' labor that you led is rolled out by the company to more than twenty projects across the province. When a new project breaks ground, the first document sent to its project office is that one.
events.e_young_workers: The workers on site keep getting older, more than half of them over fifty. Now and then someone in their twenties comes, to drive a tower crane or operate a robot, and earns more than the old hands.

c_advance.title: Advance the money or not
c_advance.situation: The rebar crew's subcontractor says this month's progress payment hasn't come, so wages will be two weeks late. But the workers are already gathering outside the prefabs, and the project manager asks what you'll do: under the regulations the general contractor can advance the wages and recover them later, but getting it past company finance won't be easy.

options.label: Write the advance request and chase it yourself
options.result: You write the request and spend three days running between company finance and the deputy in charge with the attendance and wage sheets, and on the fourth day the money reaches the dedicated account. After that, the subcontractor offers you a cigarette whenever he sees you.

options.label: Lean on the subcontractor to find a way
options.result: You call the subcontractor in and lay out the contract terms in front of the project manager. The next day he borrows the money and pays the wages, looking very unhappy.

c_cert.title: Take the Level 3 labor relations coordinator exam
c_cert.situation: The company says labor managers will be promoted first from people with the certificate; your trade sits under the labor relations coordinator occupation. Level 3 means studying labor law and mediation techniques and writing up cases, and you only have evenings and weekends.

options.label: Sign up
options.result: You study for three months in the prefab office on site, and the case you write in the exam is the night twenty-odd workers surrounded the project office.

options.label: Not yet
options.result: You think what happens on site can't be learned from books, and don't sign up. At year end, when the commendations come out, the people with certificates are listed first.

c_contractor.title: Jump to a labor subcontracting company
c_contractor.situation: A labor subcontractor you've dealt with for years wants you to be a project lead at his company, running crews of over three hundred workers, for forty percent more pay. But you know that's the side the general contractor inspects, and the side most likely to get into trouble.

options.label: Go to the subcontractor
options.result: You go from checking other people's wage sheets to being the one who makes them. In your first month you overhaul their whole attendance and payment process.

options.label: Stay with the general contractor
options.result: You say you feel more settled at the general contractor. He smiles and says then my wage sheets will still have to go past you.

c_ai_check.title: Lead the build of a data check process
c_ai_check.situation: The company wants to link real-name, gate and bank payment data, and have AI produce monthly risk alerts automatically. It wants a payroll administrator who knows the sites to set the rules: which anomalies need a site visit, which can be checked remotely. Some say one person will soon be able to run three projects.

options.label: Lead the rules
options.result: You turn every trick you've run into over the years into a rule, and spell out which things require seeing the person themselves. After the system goes live, buddy punching drops by more than half.

options.label: Look after your own project
options.result: You say what happens on site still has to be seen on site. Someone at headquarters builds the system; there are a few rules you think are wrong, and you say so in the group chat.

c_labor_manager.title: Compete for Project Labor Manager
c_labor_manager.situation: The company's big project in the Airport Economy Zone needs a Project Labor Manager to oversee a dozen subcontractors' labor, handle unpaid-wage disputes and deal with every kind of inspection. To compete you present a dispute you've handled, and answer questions in front of the project manager and several subcontractors.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: You talk about the night the subcontractor ran off, from the first worker's attendance to the last. One of the subcontractors in the room says, I was there that day.

options.label: Leave it to an older colleague
options.result: You think old Sun, with twenty years on sites, can handle people better than you, and don't apply. Once he has the job he often hands the difficult cases to you.

c_inspector.title: Become a labor inspection assistant at the human resources bureau
c_inspector.situation: The district human resources and social security bureau's labor inspection brigade is hiring assistants who know the regulations and know construction sites. You'd no longer be stuck on a site, for twenty percent less pay, and you'd switch sides to inspect other people's projects.

options.label: Become an inspection assistant
options.result: You change into different clothes, and the first time you walk onto a site as part of an inspection team, the first thing you look at is still the notice board by the gate.
options.end: You became a labor inspection assistant, going from site to site checking ledgers and dedicated accounts and asking workers questions. The people in the project offices get nervous when you come, and you know what they're nervous about.

options.label: Stay with the general contractor
options.result: You say you still want to work on sites. The brigade chief says when they inspect your projects in future, they won't have to worry.

c_hr_head.title: Go to headquarters as Company Labor / HR Supervisor
c_hr_head.situation: Company headquarters wants a labor supervisor to run the labor and payroll system and compliance for dozens of projects across the province, and later some of human resources too. It means an office, meetings and reviewing policies, and rarely going to sites anymore.

options.label: Go to headquarters
options.result: You move into the headquarters building, dozens of projects' monthly reports on your desk. The last time you watched people scan their faces at a site gate was two months ago.

options.label: Stay on the project
options.result: You say the project can't spare anyone. Headquarters sends someone else, and whenever something hard comes up, they still call to ask how you handled it back then.

c_hometown.title: Go back home to Xinyang
c_hometown.situation: Your child lives back home with the grandparents, and you go back once a month. A construction company in your home county wants you to run its labor management, for thirty percent less pay, five minutes from home.

options.label: Go home
options.result: You hand over your Zhengzhou project and go back to Xinyang. County sites are small, a hundred-odd people per project, and you run three on your own.
options.end: You went back to your home county to look after wages and contracts on a few small sites. Among the workers is the father of a primary school classmate, and on payday he brings you a bag of Xinyang Maojian tea.

options.label: Stay in Zhengzhou
options.result: You bring your child to school in Zhengzhou, and the grandparents come too. Five of you crammed into a two-bedroom flat, and it's lively.

c_dept_head.title: Become Head of the Labor Management Department
c_dept_head.situation: The group is setting up a labor management department to oversee labor policy and unpaid-wage risk across every project. Its head deals with the human resources and construction authorities, banks and the subcontractors' association, and if there's a major unpaid-wage incident, you're the first one called in.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You start writing policies, chairing coordination meetings and visiting provincial departments, and a hundred-odd organizations' people appear in your phone contacts. Every winter you still pick a few projects and go stand at the gate.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend a labor manager you trained. The first call he makes after taking over is to ask how to negotiate with a subcontractor.

endings.retire: On your last day you go back to your first site. It's long since become an estate full of people, someone walking a dog below, children riding bikes. You stand at the estate gate a while, remembering that a workers' rights notice board once stood here, and that you wrote the hotline number on it more than once.
endings.burnout: That winter, in the week before payday, you don't sleep for seven nights straight, and your stomach hurts so much you crouch down in the prefab and can't get up. The doctor orders rest, and the company moves you to the headquarters archive to look after labor records, regular hours. In the last lunar month you still look through each project's dedicated account statements.

stages: You run labor and payroll for one project on your own. Every morning you look at the gate data; in the morning you register new workers and sign their contracts, in the afternoon you review the wage sheets the subcontractors send in, and at month's end you go to the bank to pay through the dedicated account. Crew bosses, subcontractors and workers all come to you, some to reconcile, some to plead, and the attendance record in your hand is the hardest argument there is.

You oversee labor for a dozen subcontractors on a big project. Once a week you chair a subcontractor meeting on labor, attendance and labor cost transfers; every month you spot-check crews and call in subcontractors who cut corners; when the authorities inspect, the one standing at the front answering is you. Only once you've signed a wage sheet will the bank release the money.

You sit at company headquarters now, running the labor and payroll system for dozens of projects across the province. Every month you read each project's risk report, review advance requests, handle disputes that have escalated, and teach new payroll staff. Your desk holds policy documents and records of meetings with subcontractors, and when you visit a site, the project office has the ledgers laid out ahead of time.

What you set now is how the whole group hires and pays: labor policy, check procedures, the warning lines for unpaid-wage risk. Half your week is meetings, with the human resources and construction authorities, banks and the subcontractors' association, and at year end you lead the winter campaign against unpaid wages. When you do visit a site, you still look at the notice board by the gate first.
work: A new laborer comes to register with his brother's ID card, and the gate's face match fails. You take him aside, get the story out of him, and tell him to go fetch his own papers and come back tomorrow.

The carpentry crew boss turns in a wage sheet where quantities and attendance don't match: two hundred extra workdays. You go through it day by day against the construction log, draw a dozen red circles on it and send it back.

The bank returns three payments from the payment list with a digit wrong in the card number. You phone each person, have them send a photo of their bank card, and the payments go through that afternoon.

At the subcontractor meeting, the plumbing and electrical boss says this month's labor money isn't enough and wants to pay late. You lay out the contract, the transfer receipts and the dedicated account balance one by one, and in the end he says: then I'll borrow to pay.
On a spot check of the rebar crew you stop five workers at random and ask what they got last month. Four match; one says he's ¥500 short, and you phone for the crew boss on the spot.

The construction authority inspects and asks to see a departure settlement form for a worker who left three months ago. You pull it from the ledger cabinet in two minutes, his signature and thumbprint on it, and the inspector nods.

A project in another city submits an advance request double last month's amount. You don't sign right away; first you have the project office send the subcontractor's attendance and progress payment statements, and only after reading each one do you sign.
You teach twenty new payroll staff, and what you teach isn't the clauses of the regulations but how, when workers crowd around you, to get the attendance records out first.

The AI system's monthly report rates one project highest risk. You call that project's payroll administrator, and she says the gates were broken for three days. You note on the report: equipment problem, not a labor problem.
Before the winter campaign you gather every labor manager in the group and go through unpaid-wage risk project by project, until ten at night, and in the end list seven projects to watch closely.

The provincial human resources department comes to ask how the general contractor payment system is working for you. You don't talk about achievements; you talk about three places it doesn't work in practice and how you've worked around them.

A partner bank wants to connect its wage payment system to your real-name platform. You take payroll staff from two projects to test it for a month, and write five things to fix on the acceptance form.
past: You go to middle school in the countryside outside Xinyang. Your father spends most of the year away tying rebar on construction sites, home only in the last lunar month. One year he comes home empty-handed and says the labor boss ran off.

In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you get into construction management at a university in Zhengzhou. Your father says with that, you'll be the one on site managing people, not the one being managed.
Over the summer you do odd jobs on your father's site and see workers waiting outside the project office for their pay, waiting all day. You remember the board with the labor inspection number on it.
After graduation you join this construction company and are posted to a project as a labor clerk, taking workers' fingerprints and photos and signing contracts all day, sorting the roster at night.

For the first time you follow the payroll administrator through a full payment cycle on the dedicated account, from the labor cost transfer to the money landing in the bank. That night you call your father and tell him wages go straight onto the card now.
The previous payroll administrator is moved to another project, and the project manager has you step in. You take over that whole cabinet of ledgers and spend a week going through it.

late.pension_note: Estimate: thirty-odd years of contributions to Zhengzhou's basic pension for company employees on a state-owned company's wage base, plus a small company annuity, comes to about half your final monthly pay.
scenes: In the last lunar month of your first year retired, you still check your phone at month's end out of habit, waiting for someone to ask about wages. The phone is quiet.

Someone from your home village has been cheated of wages in another province and finds you through a friend. On the phone you tell him which office to go to and what evidence to bring, and a month later he calls to say he got paid.
Your child graduates from university and joins a law firm doing labor law. He says when a construction site case comes up, you're the first person he wants to ask.
You play Chinese chess in the park with a few old men, one of whom used to drive a tower crane on sites. The two of you talk all afternoon, and neither wins.
You look after records in the archive and leave on time, and slowly your stomach gets better. For the first time you eat dinner at home for a whole month.
A young payroll administrator calls: a subcontractor is about to run. You hear him out and tell him to seal all the attendance and wage sheets first, then go find the project manager.
When the time comes you retire. The cabinet of ledgers in the archive, you label book by book before handing it over.
In your first year out of the project office, whenever you pass a construction site, you glance at whether the notice board by the gate has the inspection hotline on it.
You find your footing in the new place. A rebar worker from your old project calls at New Year to say he's bought a flat in Zhengzhou now, and his kid goes to school here.
The labor clerk you trained becomes a project labor manager and sends you a photo: the new notice board at a site gate, in her own handwriting.

Later the gates, the platform and the dedicated accounts are all connected, and when wages land it's all clear on the phone. But every last lunar month, someone still has to stand at the project office door and explain the accounts item by item.

Your father has grown old and sits sunning himself in the yard. He says after that year the labor boss ran off, he was never cheated of pay again. You don't tell him how many fake wage sheets you caught in those years.

closing.retire: One winter many years later you take the high-speed train home, and the carriage is full of people with woven sacks, each looking at a bank deposit message on their phone. You watch them, then turn your face to the window.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find an old roster in a drawer. The first pages you copied by hand as a labor clerk: six hundred-odd names, each followed by a red thumbprint. You leaf through a few pages and close it again.
closing.end: Many years later you pass that estate on the east side of Zhengzhou. Outside the supermarket below, a few old people are chatting in the Zhoukou dialect. You stand by the road a while, and don't go over to say hello.
